title: Oscar and the Garden
premise: Orsen Lockridge has spent his life as the quiet keeper of a gate in a valley where magic cannot enter, tending a garden that remembers things he cannot. When the old gods resume answering prayers, their returning power begins to erode the valley's protection—and with it, Orsen's false memories of who he is. He learns he is not the gate's keeper but its lock: a living seal created from a forgotten prince to imprison a god that once devoured prayers. To save the found family that has gathered around him, Orsen must leave the valley, cross a country that was erased from every map and memory, and find the original door—choosing at last between dissolving himself to renew the seal or breaking it and facing the god as a whole man. In the end he does neither: he plants the garden at the threshold, making the door a place instead of a prison, and walks home changed but whole.
about_author: Bram Winterbourne is the pen name of a former botanist who spent a decade cataloguing heirloom seeds in remote valleys before turning to fiction. Their novels blend folkloric fantasy with quiet meditations on memory, belonging, and the landscapes that hold us together.

chapters.title: The Gate That Stays Shut
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. We meet him tending the walled garden beside an iron gate no one opens, in a valley where candles won't flicker with magic and prayers go unanswered. His neighbor Maren brings bread; her daughter Wren follows him everywhere like a shadow. The beat is gentle routine hiding a low hum of wrongness—the garden blooms out of season.

chapters.title: First Answered Prayer
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Wren prays for rain during a drought, and it rains—hard, unnatural, smelling of something older than weather. The valley's protective hush stutters. Orsen feels the gate hum under his palm for the first time. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread as the impossible becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: What the Garden Remembers
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Plants in the garden begin growing into shapes: a crown, a burning city, a woman's face. Orsen realizes the flowers are blooming memories—not his own. Maren admits she found him as a young man at the gate with no past. Beat: the vertigo of learning your history may be a lie.

chapters.title: The Pilgrim at the Wall
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A ragged pilgrim named Sable arrives claiming the old gods woke when someone 'stopped holding the door.' She recognizes the gate's sigil tattooed faintly on Orsen's wrist—a mark he thought was a birthmark. Beat: first confirmation he is bound to something vast.

chapters.title: Wren Sees the Door
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The child sees what adults can't: a second door shimmering inside the iron one, and behind Orsen, a tall shadow wearing his silhouette. She loves him anyway. Beat: tenderness and terror braided; the reader learns the threat wears Orsen's shape.

chapters.title: The Valley Forgets a Village
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The neighboring hamlet of Alderbrook simply ceases—houses remain, but no one recalls anyone who lived there. Sable explains: the returning god eats memory to rebuild itself, starting at the edges of sealed places. Beat: stakes become intimate and irreversible.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Confession
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren reveals the letter left with Orsen decades ago, written by his predecessor: 'He is not the keeper. He is the lock.' She chose family over duty and never told him. Beat: guilt, love, and betrayal tangled; found family strained by a protective lie.

chapters.title: Country Without a Name
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Researching the erased country in the chapel's buried archive, Orsen finds maps that unwrite themselves as he reads. The nation of Vessany was sacrificed to make the prison; its people became the seal's mortar. Beat: grief for a homeland he never knew was his.

chapters.title: Leaving the Valley
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The group—Orsen, Sable, Maren, Wren—slips through the gate at moonset, the only hour it permits passage. Crossing the threshold, magic floods Orsen like cold water, and half his false memories burn away. Beat: painful liberation; identity stripped to bone.

chapters.title: Roads That Argue Back
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. In Vessany's ghost-country, roads rearrange to keep travelers lost, and prayer-shrines whisper offers. Sable confesses she serves a rival god who wants the prisoner freed. Beat: trust fractures within the party; alliances revealed as transactions.

chapters.title: The Inn of Borrowed Names
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The party shelters at an inn staffed by the erased dead of Vessany, who trade hospitality for being remembered. Maren memorizes their names all night. Beat: warmth amid horror; the theme of memory as an act of love made literal.

chapters.title: Wren Bargains with a God
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A small god of thresholds offers Wren safe passage in exchange for 'the person you'll miss most.' Clever child that she is, she gives it a pressed flower from Orsen's garden instead. Beat: hope and ingenuity; the gods can be outwitted by sincerity.

chapters.title: The Prince in the Well
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. At a ruined well, reflections show Orsen's true face: Prince Aurel of Vessany, who volunteered to be unmade so his people could be woven into the seal. The devourer-god speaks through the water: 'Come unlock me, little lock.' Beat: identity crisis peaks—he was complicit in his own erasure.

chapters.title: Sable's Betrayal
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable leads the party into a trap meant to open Orsen like a key. But seeing Wren's fear, she turns her blade on her own god's servant instead. Beat: redemption purchased at cost; Sable is gravely wounded, and the party must carry her.

chapters.title: The Devourer's Court
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Captured anyway by the god's hunger-storms, Orsen stands in a court built from eaten prayers, where the devourer shows him every life he might have had if he'd stayed sealed and ignorant. Beat: temptation rendered as mercy; the cruelest offer is comfort.

chapters.title: What Maren Carried
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren confronts the god with the one thing it cannot digest: ordinary, stubborn, imperfect human memory—burnt bread, scraped knees, arguments forgiven. Her testimony cracks the court's illusion. Beat: the thesis stated in action; small love defeats grand hunger.

chapters.title: The Original Door
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The party reaches the First Door beneath Vessany's drowned capital. It requires a whole soul willingly given. Orsen prepares to dissolve himself back into the seal. Beat: darkest moment—sacrifice framed as the only honest ending.

chapters.title: Wren Refuses the Ending
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren refuses to let Orsen go, and plants garden seeds at the Door's threshold, insisting doors should be gardens, not graves. The erased dead of the inn arrive, remembered now by name, lending their voices. Beat: rebellion against narrative fate; found family as counter-magic.

chapters.title: A Place Instead of a Prison
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Climax. Orsen chooses a third path: he feeds the seal his false memories—the invented keeper's life—rather than his soul, and invites the devourer to be gardened rather than caged. The god, starved for eons of anything genuine, accepts cultivation over consumption. Beat: transformation of the antagonist through offered intimacy.

chapters.title: Rain Over Vessany
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV shifts. The erased country floods back into the world's memory; names return to mouths, roads settle, the dead innkeepers wake in sunlight. The old gods recede to shrines and small favors. Beat: catharsis; restoration without erasing the cost.

chapters.title: The Gardener Returns
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen comes home to the valley carrying cuttings from the First Door's garden. He is Aurel and Orsen both, and chooses the name his family gave him. The gate stays shut, but now because it's a door to a tended place, not a prison. Beat: integration; identity chosen, not assigned.

chapters.title: Seeds for Next Spring
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, years later. Wren, now the valley's new keeper-in-training, writes letters to faraway friends about a garden where even gods come to rest. Orsen teaches her pruning, patience, and which flowers remember. Final beat: legacy, continuity, and peace—the found family endures beyond the story's end.
